questions.q: What are the four parts of a strong answer to a challenge from a stakeholder?
options: Deny, defend, deflect, defer
Answer in one sentence, give evidence, concede what is true in the objection, name a next step
Show the code, show the model, show the chart, show the appendix
Agree, apologize, promise, repeat
questions.explain: Conceding shows you have seen the weakness before they did, and the next step turns the objection into a plan.

questions.q: Average precision was 0.338 on training rows, 0.327 in cross-validation, and 0.334 on the test set. How does this answer 'is it overfit?'
options: It proves the model is perfect
The test set is always lower than training
It does not answer the question at all
The three scores are within about 0.01; a model that memorized its training data would score much higher in-sample than on unseen data
questions.explain: Overfitting shows up as a large gap between training and held-out performance. There is no such gap here, though it does not test a later period.

questions.q: Choosing the same 369 customers by 'days since last order' gave precision 0.187 and a net of -567 per cycle, while the model gave 0.401 and 5,121. What does this show?
options: Simple rules are always better
Net value does not depend on precision
The model earns about three times what the better rule earns, and the intuitive rule falls below the 20.8% break-even and loses money
The break-even changes with the rule
questions.explain: A precision below the break-even means each contact costs more than it earns, so the intuitive rule loses money. The comparison uses the same 369 contacts and the same illustrative economics.

questions.q: Premium customers were flagged at 22.1% while Family customers were flagged at 3.8%. How should you respond to a fairness question about this?
options: Explain that it follows the groups' real churn rates (21.4% vs 11.5%), show that precision on the list is similar across groups, and note the limits of the check
Deny that any difference exists
Remove the plan feature and say no more
Say the model cannot be checked by group
questions.explain: A group check asks who is flagged and whether the list is right equally often. Differences that follow real risk are explainable; the honest answer also states what the check does not cover.

questions.q: The pilot sizing showed about 241 customers per arm for a 30% save rate but over 1,000 per arm for a 15% save rate. What does this imply?
options: Smaller effects are easier to detect
Pilots are unnecessary
One cycle's list of 369 (about 185 per arm) is too small even for a 30% effect, and small effects need much larger pilots
The model must be wrong
questions.explain: Detecting a smaller effect needs many more customers. Plan the pilot across the top two deciles or across two cycles, and be honest that a small effect is expensive to rule out.
